chapter: Lucky Roberts, Armstrong and the big-band rivalries
title: Ellington on radio from the Cotton Club and battles of bands at the Savoy
summary: Musicians heard Ellington only on the radio from the Cotton Club until the Savoy Ballroom battles with Henderson, where Tricky Sam growled the St. Louis Blues.

story.theme_name: Playing with Count Basie: joining, leading, leaving

blocks.x: You know, Rex Stewart had in his book, Jazz Masters of the 1930's that initially because the guys of the Ellington Band were playing the Cotton Club and people didn't like the Cotton Club because of its racial policies, he said at first the guys tried to kind of write the band off, you know, they just kind of didn't pay much attention to him. But then big guys like Johnny Hodges and Barney Bigard and others started coming around to the Rhythm Club and other places and started jamming, you know.

Yeah, because the only way they could hear them was on the radio. And when they started hearing them on that radio, they understood. They had to understand, man. They had to understand. This was them. And on the radio every night from the Cotton Club and therefore -- there wasn't no band could touch them. Fletcher was downtown. Fletcher was downtown playing these waltzes and everything else. So the only time you could hear them in person was at the Savoy Ballroom when they had that battle. That's the only time you could hear them in person.

And it was two heavyweights there together.
Are you talking about those battles of the bands?
Oh, sure, sure. You've got to see them. the I played in relief's band (PROTESTIC) a lot of times up there.

They would get up there, Tricky Sam would get up there and play the "St. Louis Blues" and start growling up there, you've got to go. And then when Fletcher would start playing the "D Natural Stomp" and the "King Porter Stomp", you've got to go. They started fanning those derbies and that brass was up there, you've got to go. That's it. One as great as the other one, that's the way to go.
